Final response to reviewer: Thanks. The rapid review was not designed to extract information on research incentives, so there is no systematic data on this, but several included studies report how they paid participants: What and how much: mostly gift cards or vouchers, in small amounts tied to specific research tasks. In a proof-of-concept study of a single 90-minute laboratory session, in which men practised romantic conversations with a GPT-4o-based chatbot while a therapist was present, participants received a CA$40 gift card after the session (which ended with a short questionnaire) and CA$30 after completing the final follow-up questionnaire three months later (Lafortune et al. 2026, https://doi.org/10.1007/s10508-025-03356-3). In a pilot of a 14-day CBT programme for health anxiety, delivered by a decision tree–based chatbot on Facebook Messenger in daily 5–10-minute modules, each completed questionnaire (post-intervention and 12-week follow-up) earned one entry in a prize draw for one of five NZ$50 retail vouchers, with additional entries for completing an interview (Goonesekera and Donkin 2022, https://doi.org/10.2196/37877). In the one South African study, young men who have sex with men and transgender women used a GPT-4-based counselling chatbot (an introductory problem-solving module based on the Friendship Bench) in a single 20–30-minute session on a study laptop, followed by a 60–90-minute interview or focus group discussion; participants were reimbursed R160 “for their time, inconvenience and travel” (Humphries et al. 2026, https://doi.org/10.1093/trstmh/traf143). Some studies also paid for using the intervention, not only for research tasks. In a 7-day study of a suite of brief stress-management chatbots on Telegram, participants received a US$10 gift card for completing both the pre- and post-study questionnaires, plus US$3 for each day they used the chatbots and completed a daily survey (prorated for partial completion), and US$25 per hour for an optional interview (Mauriello et al. 2021, https://doi.org/10.2196/25294). In a 6-module CBT programme for generalised anxiety, used over up to 9 weeks through a smartphone app with a conversational agent delivering pre-written clinician responses and human support, participants received vouchers of up to £60 in total based on study assessments and completion of modules, plus a £15 voucher per interview attended (Papiernik et al. 2025, https://doi.org/10.2196/76377). In a 2-week pilot of a generative AI (large language model–based) mental wellness chatbot app, participants were paid US$50 a week for at least 60 minutes of chatbot use, or US$30 for more than 30 minutes, with further payments for surveys and interviews, up to US$275 in total (Graupensperger et al. 2026, https://doi.org/10.2196/90644). When: after each completed research task (a session, questionnaire, follow-up assessment or interview), sometimes prorated for partial completion, or as a total at the end of the study. Who handles: rarely reported. In two trials the developer covered the cost of incentives (Fitzpatrick et al. 2017, https://doi.org/10.2196/mental.7785; Fulmer et al. 2018, https://doi.org/10.2196/mental.9782), and in the first of these the university made the payments; in another trial a university institute funded participant payments (Vowels et al. 2025, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmen.0000411). Caution for the trial design: two studies that paid for chatbot use reported problems with this. In one, some participants said they used the app mainly to reach the payment threshold; the authors note that engagement figures reflect the study protocol rather than voluntary use, and that the incentives may also have influenced self-reported outcomes (Graupensperger et al. 2026, https://doi.org/10.2196/90644). In the other, the authors note that the payment scheme encouraged off-topic use of the chatbots and likely influenced participant behaviour (Mauriello et al. 2021, https://doi.org/10.2196/25294). Linking MHAA trial incentives to completing research assessments, equally in both arms, rather than to using MHAA, would avoid inflating engagement figures. No included study compared incentive amounts or schedules, or described how payments were administered or documented. These details will need to come from UCT and South African ethics requirements, alongside the BJPsych Open paper shared, which was not part of our review.
